entities.summary:
Maurice de Sully, Bishop of Paris from 1160 until his retirement in 1196, stands as a monumental figure in French medieval history, primarily celebrated as the visionary behind the Cathedral of Notre-Dame de Paris. Born into humble origins in Sully-sur-Loire around the early 12th century, his intellectual acumen and administrative prowess propelled him through the ecclesiastical ranks, culminating in his election to the prestigious Parisian see. His episcopacy coincided with a period of burgeoning Capetian power under Louis VII and Philip II Augustus, and a flourishing of urban development in Paris, for which Sully envisioned a cathedral commensurate with the city's growing importance as a royal and intellectual capital.

The genesis of Notre-Dame began in 1163 when Pope Alexander III laid the foundation stone, initiating one of the most ambitious construction projects of the High Middle Ages. Sully personally oversaw the design, a radical departure from the Romanesque style, embracing the nascent Gothic principles of ribbed vaults, flying buttresses (though later perfected), and expansive stained-glass windows. Under his direction, the choir and nave were substantially completed, embodying a synthesis of structural innovation and spiritual aspiration. Beyond the cathedral, Sully was a diligent administrator, reforming diocesan governance, establishing schools, and participating in significant political and ecclesiastical events, including the preparations for the Third Crusade.
